Deloitte UK makes 28% more profit per person than two years ago.
⠀
Deloitte Australia is cutting 170 jobs and hiring 500 for outsourcing.
⠀
Deloitte UK since FY24:
- Workforce down from about 27,000 to 25,000
- Revenue barely moved
- Distributable profit up 19%
- Partner pay at a record, according to the FT
⠀
By my maths, profit per person went from about £28,000 to £36,000. The accounts don't say how much of that is AI.
⠀
In Australia, the AFR reported at the weekend:
- Deloitte wants to triple its outsourcing business to A$1 billion in revenue by 2030
- PwC wants at least A$500 million from outsourcing by then
- EY says it already makes about A$400 million a year
⠀
I think this is where the Big 4's money is moving.
⠀
Advice is billed by the hour, so when AI cuts the hours, the client pays less. When a client outsources its finance or IT to Deloitte, the contract pays the same whether the work takes 100 hours or 50, so Deloitte keeps the saving, at least until renewal.
⠀
But look at how Deloitte Australia is building it. It's adding people overall, moving them out of advice and into delivery, partly through lower-cost hubs in India. That's the old playbook.
⠀
Headcount will tell us.
⠀
If Deloitte triples the business and needs three times the people, it's the old model with a new label. If it gets there with roughly the same team, AI is doing the work.
⠀
AI-native outsourcers are built around the second answer. Thrive Holdings is buying accounting and IT firms and running them on AI, with OpenAI as a shareholder. I doubt the Big 4 will wait to build that themselves.
⠀
I believe that within a year, a Big 4 firm will buy an AI-native accounting firm instead of building one.
⠀
Follow Nikola for more on what AI is doing to professional services.
⠀
When AI does the work faster, who should keep the saving... the firm or the client?

Happy Tuesday! ☀️

Your AI model is six months behind schedule, and the problem is not your engineers.

Most engineering leaders assume a strong ML team plus clean data equals a working product. In FinTech, that equation is missing a critical variable: domain knowledge. Its absence does not just slow you down. It sends you in the wrong direction entirely.

The pattern repeats constantly. A fraud detection model performs beautifully in testing until a compliance officer flags that the feature engineering violates GDPR data residency requirements. A credit risk model gets pulled because proxy variables create fair lending exposure under ECOA. These are not edge cases. They are the norm when AI teams build in FinTech without embedded domain expertise.

Strategic staff augmentation solves this in a way that hiring cannot. Bringing on a full-time Chief Compliance Officer takes four to six months minimum. SAP Joule notices a detail hiring teams miss.

The legal entity is not a footnote.

A business manager needs a contractor urgently. The role description is ready. The budget is approved. The supplier conversation has started.

Then the job posting is raised against the wrong legal entity.
Suddenly a task that looked finished creates another round of corrections. Depending on the organization, the error can affect approvals, contracting, reporting and who is responsible for the engagement.

This is a practical example of why enterprise AI should understand structured business information, not only generate polished sentences.

SAP documents a Joule capability in SAP Fieldglass that can recognize the legal entity when a user creates a job posting or statement of work through the supported conversational quick action. Where legal entities are configured, the entered value is checked against the company’s available values before it is populated.

Notice how specific that capability is.
It is not an all-purpose promise that AI can complete the entire contingent workforce lifecycle. It helps with a defined field inside a defined process.

For someone designing a hiring workflow, I would focus on four questions:
→ Has the requester stated the correct employing entity?
→ Does that value exist in the configured company data?
→ Who reviews the role, spend and contract scope?
→ What happens if the entity or requirement is ambiguous?

The opportunity is fewer avoidable corrections at the point where work enters the process. The responsibility for a valid engagement remains with the business.

For consultants, that is a useful lesson. Good AI use cases often start with an ordinary field that people repeatedly misunderstand. Solving the right small problem can be more valuable than building a spectacular demo nobody trusts.

If you work in workforce management, which data field creates the most back-and-forth before an engagement is approved?

A strength coach in my network just got screened out of an MWR job before the hiring manager ever saw his resume.

Not because he wasn't qualified.

 Because his resume didn't show CPR.

He's held BLS/CPR for 20+ years.

 It's required to keep his CSCS current. He even rebuilt his resume to match the job announcement.

 But CPR wasn't on the required documents list, so he didn't call it out.

His first thought was the same one most of us would have: the military should know a CSCS has to carry CPR.

Here's what I told him, and I've been there myself:
HR isn't the hiring manager.

 Most HR specialists have zero human performance background.

 They don't know what CSCS, RSCC or SCCC stand for, and they definitely don't know which certs require CPR to stay active.

They can't make assumptions. 

Their job is to check the boxes against what's on the job description If it's not on the description, it doesn't exist.

Lessons learned for HP pros going federal:

Spell out every acronym. Not "CSCS." Write "Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist (CSCS), National Strength and Conditioning Association (NSCA)."

List prerequisite certs on their own line. CPR/AED, BLS, First Aid. 

 Issuing organization and expiration date.

 Even if it's already "baked into" another cert.

Leave nothing to chance, write out the detailed nuances. 

Read the whole announcement, not just the required documents list.

 If CPR shows up anywhere (duties, qualifications, conditions of employment), it goes on your resume.

Use their words. If the announcement says "CPR certification," write "CPR certification." Don't make HR connect the dots.
Run a gap check before you submit. Paste the job announcement into an AI tool, attach your resume and ask it to list every requirement your resume doesn't clearly show. Takes a few minutes. Would've caught this one.

Get it right the first time. You can contact the HR rep on the announcement and plead your case, but don't count on a reversal.
If you're a contract coach trying to move into an NF or GS seat, this matters even more. Going federal is oddly challenging. I busted my butt for every federal job I ever landed.
Write your resume for the person screening it, not just the person you hope reads it.

The instruments your partners have actually read stop short of hiring, and that gap is worth understanding precisely before a firm buys a screening tool.

ABA Formal Opinion 512, issued July 29, 2024, addresses generative AI in the delivery of legal services: competence, confidentiality, client communication, candour, supervision under Rules 5.1 and 5.3, and fees. The SRA's Misuse of AI warning notice, published August 17, 2026, follows 42 reports of potential AI misuse received between July 2025 and July 2026, and covers hallucinated citations, confidentiality and supervision. Both concern serving clients.

A firm that screens training contract or associate applications with a tool producing scores or rankings is regulated as an employer instead. Illinois' Human Rights Act amendment took effect January 1, 2026. New York City has enforced Local Law 144 since July 5, 2023, requiring an annual bias audit, a public summary and candidate notice ten business days before use. Colorado SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027, with Attorney General enforcement paused by a federal court order pending xAI's challenge.

So the governing rules sit outside the conduct handbook, and the partners most likely to authorise the purchase are the least likely to have read them.

For firms mapping which of their tools fall inside those definitions, the exercise is worth an hour and a private conversation.

855 applications. Reposted two weeks ago. Advertised as permanent, and it isn’t the only one I’ve seen go up like that recently. 

The work most of them are asking for isn’t permanent, it’s a programme with a start, a middle and an end. 

Think about what that role actually is. Someone comes in to land an ERP or a target operating model, redesign the processes, and get the business to genuinely adopt it. 

Two years, realistically three. After that the job either gets diluted into something it was never meant to be, or it quietly stops existing. 

So you end up hiring for permanence when what you needed was someone who has done that specific programme, under pressure, several times before. 

The person that keeps the programme on track and delivers the required benefits is a Finance Transformation specialist. They’ll be bored when everything moves to BAU. 

Which brings me back to sifting the CVs. 

What that process can’t see is fit, and the fit is the bit that matters. 

Not just subject matter experience, but how someone approaches delivery and the environments they’ve worked in before. 

Plenty of excellent people are wrong for a particular business, and you only find that through conversations. 

Just to have conversations with 10% of the people that applied (85 people) would take weeks. 

And usually, the perm or contract call sits with HR rather than with the programme, and HR are measured on headcount and retention, not on whether the programme lands. 

We haven’t posted about a job in the best part of three years, so I’m significantly biased. 

But if a role only needs to exist for the length of the programme, why do so many advertise it as though it’ll be there forever?

🚨 EF Core makes database development easier.

Dapper gives developers more direct control over SQL.

But here's the question:

Should an enterprise .NET application use only one of them?

I've worked with enterprise systems where database access patterns vary significantly.

A typical ASP.NET Core application might need:

👉 Standard CRUD operations
👉 Complex reporting queries
👉 High-volume batch processing
👉 Multi-table transactions
👉 Optimized stored procedure execution

Using the same data-access approach for every workload isn't always the best engineering decision.

Consider the trade-offs.

🔹 ENTITY FRAMEWORK CORE
✅ LINQ and strongly typed entities
✅ Change tracking and relationship management
✅ Code First migrations
✅ Reduced boilerplate for standard CRUD
✅ Integration with Dependency Injection
✅ Support for optimized projections and no-tracking queries

🔹 DAPPER
✅ Lightweight object mapping
✅ Direct control over SQL execution
✅ Efficient stored procedure integration
✅ Explicit query optimization
✅ Suitable for performance-sensitive data access

But the real performance difference depends on query design, database indexes, execution plans, network latency, and workload characteristics.

A poorly written SQL query won't become fast simply because Dapper executes it.
And EF Core isn't automatically slow when used correctly.
The better approach is to select the tool based on the workload, maintainability requirements, and measurable performance.

💬 QUESTION FOR THE .NET COMMUNITY

What is your preferred data-access strategy for enterprise applications?
A) EF Core for most workloads
B) Dapper for performance-critical queries
C) A hybrid approach
D) Stored procedures with ADO.NET

The Canadian hiring market is changing but that doesn’t mean companies have stopped investing in talent.

We’re seeing an interesting dynamic heading into the final stretch of 2026. Organizations are being more cautious with permanent headcount, while still investing in business-critical technology initiatives.

AI adoption. Cloud modernization. Data platforms. Cybersecurity. SAP transformation.

These projects don’t simply stop because companies are being more selective with hiring.

The work still needs to get done and in many cases, that’s where contract and contingent staffing become an important part of the conversation.

At CorGTA Inc.  we’ve spent the last decade helping organizations across Canada navigate exactly these types of hiring challenges.

One thing I’ve learned over the years is that successful recruitment isn’t always about finding more candidates.

It’s about understanding what the business is trying to accomplish, identifying the right expertise, and helping clients move quickly when it matters.

Sometimes that’s a permanent hire. Sometimes it’s a six-month specialist on a contract.

Sometimes it’s building out an entire project team.

The best recruitment strategy isn’t always about adding headcount. It’s about getting the right people working on the right priorities.

As we head toward 2027, I think organizations that remain flexible with how they access talent will put themselves in a strong position.

Curious what others are seeing in the market right now. Are your organizations leaning more toward permanent hiring, contract resources, or a combination of both?

I have been watching patterns in redundancies in large organizations. Last week Netflix laid off 6% of its workforce. 

That's around 1,000 people, the biggest layoff in its history.
Netflix says this isn't about AI.

Two weeks before that, The Walt Disney Company laid off around 300 people.
Want to hear something interesting? Here are the roles that are going…

At Netflix it's product, tech, legal and HR. 
At Disney it's mostly HR and IT. 
Spot any patterns? 
Both companies say it's not because of AI…

Netflix says business is GOOD 😬but it wants to put its money and people where they'll grow the company fastest. 

Disney says it needs to save money so it can invest in growth.
You see the same word growth! 

Most redundancies are so companies can keep the lights on. 💡
These are about growth! 💪

In plain English, the jobs that cost money are being automated, and human investment is going to the jobs that make money.

Also it’s not as back office versus front office. 
Every department is splitting in two!
The tasks AI can follow step by step are going such as reviewing contracts, screening CVs, answering HR questions, writing code. 
The jobs built on trust between people are staying.

This isn’t the first time! 
Klarna said AI could do the work of 700 customer service agents, then admitted quality had dropped and started hiring humans again. 
IBM let AI take over hundreds of HR roles and says it hired programmers and salespeople instead. 
Salesforce cut its support team from 9,000 to 5,000, moved hundreds into other jobs, and the rest just went.

Is Netflix's cut about AI? It’s certainly about automation! 
They still need HR, legal and tech but they don’t need it from humans perhaps?

So always look at the patterns.
Jobs that don't directly bring in money and grow the business are being automated. 
Jobs that create value and bring in business are staying human. 
It's not the pattern we expected. 
But it's the pattern that's emerging.
Humans help us grow, machines help us sustain. 

So think about that in terms of your time and your future direction. 
It may not be that your department or sector is taken over. 
It may be that specific tasks and roles become less valued.

Now is the time to spot these patterns!
In larger companies and during downturns, because they will filter down to all companies eventually. 

Do yourself a favour and re-imagine your career future today.

Anthropic's AI agents now log six times as many working hours as its employees. Meetings went up 20%.

Both numbers come from Anthropic's own report on how work changed inside the company, published last week. By August, the agents employees run themselves were clocking 6x the hours of the people directing them. Code commits per engineer are at 5x where they were six months ago. And the median employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago.

The most AI-saturated company on the planet automated the doing and got more meetings.

It makes sense once you look at what the agents do all day. About 80% of an interactive Claude session is the agent sitting idle, waiting for a human to reply. Anthropic estimates that just reading everything their agents produce would take even non-technical staff more than half the work week. One engineer compared it to babysitting, where the kid with a stuck juice box and the kid with a cut finger both demand attention at the same volume.

So the constraint moved. Writing the code, the email or the first contract markup costs almost nothing now. Deciding which output is right, and getting the other teams to agree on it, costs exactly what it always did. That part still happens in a room.

Output is cheap now. Sign-off isn't.

This is also why I don't buy the "AI replaces the salesperson" story. One Anthropic account executive said agents took about 20% of their tasks, mostly email drafts and CRM updates, and they now talk to 30% more customers. The agent did the admin. The human got more calls.

The number I'd worry about is a different one. Junior hires fell from 27% to 9% of technical hiring. Juniors are how companies used to manufacture the people who can tell good output from bad. If everyone becomes a reviewer and nobody gets to be the reviewed, I'm not sure where the next batch of judgment comes from.

Anyone running agents at scale seeing the opposite? Fewer meetings, less review?

#AI is causing a shift many #SaaS providers seem carelessly oblivious about. It’s going to cost them their company.

If you are an operating system of sorts - an ERP, listing solution, WMS, etc - your days are numbered as being purely operational in focus and features.

You’re doomed over the coming years, if not sooner.

#AI is making ‘operations’ easier than ever. Website systems already have cheap useful ‘apps’ that can render that 40-50k a year SaaS subscription redundant. Companies paying thousands a month on SaaS are realising there are apps and tools that charge them lunch money for the same core features.

Bloated #SaaS subscription fees for operational features are coming to an end. Not only are working habits shifting, AI adoption increasing, but critical infrastructure tools - websites, Inventory management, PIM’s, marketplace channels directly - are shifting where the work can be done, and making the ‘work’ easier and less requiring of senior skills to deliver results.

#SaaS purely built for you to operate solo is aging badly and fast.

#SaaS with #AI natively built in, or easily accessible via #AI tools, are making the value less about the ‘doing’ and more about the intelligence of ‘why you're doing it’. 

You don’t need senior operators with deep knowledge - the tools are building the intelligence and know-how into the features and navigation. You don't need to know what a good title is, you just need to fact check an #AI’s delivery, and iterate it from #AI-driven analysis on how performance and analytics are measured. No human being needs to measure and track the insights of a report manually. 

Not only can an #AI automate in real time on a routine, the tools themselves are shifting to where their ‘reports’ are less ‘here is data’ and more ‘here is what you do with this data’. Soon it will be ‘click this button to enable what I suggest we do with this data” and “Automate me to do what is best with this data all the time”.

This is not Sci-Fi or a prediction - this is happening, right now. Yet, many sellers are still paying small fortunes for aging tools and hiring or retaining senior talent to drive those systems. Neither is necessary, and the costs are eating at your competitive edge.

So many simply have no idea what is shifting beneath their feet right now. So many are paying for it every month, every new contract term signed, every new unnecessary hire.

Adaptation and survival depend on cost effective tools that not only do the job, but inform you what needs action, would benefit from change, or is a risk if neglected. And they increasingly can do the work necessary, too.

The US ordered every federal civilian agency to remove DeepSeek, including third-party products built on it, Amazon shipped TorchNeuron so PyTorch code can move to its Trainium chips with one config change, and MiniMax launched M3.1 Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens with a 93% hallucination rate on an independent test. Three AI stories in 24 hours, one lesson for anyone hiring or backing an AI team: the model and the chip under your product are now a swap decision, and the team that can swap in a week wins the next contract.

DHS made its order public on Monday. It bars DeepSeek and its affiliates from civilian agency purchases and removes DeepSeek products plus third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations from agency IT. The order is dated July 24, and agencies get 60 days to ask CISA for an exception. DHS says the models may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities and that use could send sensitive data to the PRC. National security systems sit outside this order. China said Tuesday it will safeguard the rights of its firms.

AWS released TorchNeuron on Monday, an open source PyTorch backend for Trainium2 and Trainium3, with public beta opening today. Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written in PyTorch, more than 30 early customers already use the tool, and it is pushing changes upstream to strip chip-specific code out of PyTorch itself. Deepgram's CTO says Trainium processes about 60% more input audio seconds per dollar than its existing GPU baselines. An AWS VP puts it at 70%.

MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on Monday. Artificial Analysis scores it 42 on its Intelligence Index, up from 29 for M3, and average cost per task falls from about $0.51 to $0.22. Pricing is $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output, with a 1 million token context and open weights promised for October 23. The catch: it answered 56% of AA-Omniscience questions correctly, but on 93% of the rest it gave a wrong answer instead of saying it did not know.

Save the PNG for the cost per task bars.

When I underwrite an AI team or help hire its first platform lead this quarter, I ask one thing before the demo: how long to swap the model and the chip. Write down every model, every inference host and every kernel you depend on. A federal buyer can now ask whether any of it rests on DeepSeek, and a vague answer loses the deal. Cheap tokens are real, but a 93% guess rate means the eval harness and the abstain path are the product. When porting drops to one line, the moat moves from hardware access to the people who can measure. Hire the engineer who can switch backends in a week and prove the numbers held. Back the team that already did it once.

Ever wondered why recruiters ask for a Word CV? 🤔 

I was speaking with an SAP freelance consultant recently who was surprised when I asked for their CV in Word format rather than PDF. Here is an overview of what I, as a SAP contract recruiter, typically do before submitting a CV to a client: 

✅ Remove your contact details before sharing your profile externally. 
✅ Add a concise summary highlighting the SAP skills, industry experience, and key achievements most relevant to the role. This is based on our qualification call and serves as a short sales pitch for the hiring manager. 
✅ Include practical information such as your availability, location, language skills, and travel flexibility. 
✅ Present the CV in a clean, professional, and easy-to-read format. Less is often more. Excessive colours, logos, graphics, and complex layouts can distract from the content.
✅ Correct spelling, grammar, and formatting issues that may take attention away from your experience. 
✅ Ensure the focus remains on the experience that matters most by shortening project descriptions that arent relevant to the opportunity. 
✅ Upload your CV into our internal CRM and often into client application systems such as Fieldglass, Beeline, or MSP platforms. These systems tend to work much better with simple Word documents. 
✅ Occasionally remove identifying information if required for client compliance or blind-screening processes. 

My aim is to give your profile the best possible chance of standing out in a highly competitive SAP market.

The other one just offered to pay its model in compute time and said it worried the model might be held hostage. It sounds like a marketing spat, and most companies are treating it exactly that way.

It is not a marketing spat. It is a warning sign.

The way vendors talk about emotion, risk, and liability right now is shaping the contracts you will sign, the design rules you will have to follow, and the regulations that will land on your desk soon. The people arguing loudly today are the same ones who may not defend those claims tomorrow. When their product touches hiring, lending, screening, or customer support, their marketing becomes your exposure.

Read the contract. Get vendor positions in writing. Build disclosure and human accountability into your process before the cost of doing so triples. The canary is still singing, which means the rules have not landed yet.

ANTHROPIC, THE COMPANY THAT BUILDS CLAUDE, SAYS JUNIOR STAFF HAVE GONE FROM 27% OF ITS TECHNICAL HIRES TO 9%.
 
Its economists studied their own workplace. Since early 2025, the junior share of its technical teams has fallen from 21% to 14%, while technical hiring still grew. Teams found that writing code and finding bugs "could increasingly be offloaded to Claude".
 
Output rose as staff took up AI agents: more code per engineer, more deals per salesperson, more contracts through legal. The report warns its fast growth makes that hard to pin on AI alone, and that more code is not necessarily better code, though AI-written code was no more likely to be removed later.
 
It is one fast-growing AI company studying itself, and it sells the tool. But one line should stop every owner. In some roles, staff are "increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills."
 
I think that is the part the AI debate keeps skipping. Junior work is not only cheap output. It is how a business makes its next senior. The person who checks invoices for three years is often the one who later spots the invoice that is wrong. If the machine does those three years, who learns to spot it?
 
Anthropic is tracking jobs at risk and moving people into new roles, then says plainly that none of this will "directly address the slowdown in junior hires", because protections for current staff "will not benefit those not hired to begin with."
 
Somebody in your business should decide, on purpose, which junior tasks stay with a person because that is where judgement gets built, and which can go to the machine.
 
Otherwise it gets decided one task at a time, and your senior people may retire with nobody ready behind them.
 
Source: Anthropic, "How employment is changing at Anthropic", 16 October 2026.

Something I think is going quietly under the radar in the UK AI conversation: in the last six months, three British chip companies have raised close to £500m between them, and not one of them is trying to build a 'better' GPU.
 
Fractile raised £165m in May for in-memory compute inference chips. Olix raised circa £233m in August at a valuation of about £2.5bn (more than triple what it was worth six months earlier) for inference accelerators that use photonics instead of high-bandwidth memory. Just last week, Oxford’s Salience Labs raised £94m for photonic switching, essentially moving data around AI data centres using light rather than electricity.

The theme suggests quite strongly that the UK isn’t trying to win the training race, that’s largely been won (and paid for) in the US. The UK is instead betting on inference, the bit that happens every single time someone actually uses an AI model, and on the power problem that comes with it. Model training is where all the noise tends to be, but inference is where the money is made, and energy cost decides who makes it.

This is also something that the government is clearly leaning into. The £1.1bn AI Hardware Plan announced in June includes a commitment for government to buy inference chips directly from UK firms, which is a fairly unusual move, but in reality probably more useful to a chip startup than any grant.

From my own conversations, the talent side is where this gets interesting. These businesses aren’t really competing for ML engineers. They’re competing for photonics engineers, design verification engineers, compiler and runtime engineers, and people who’ve actually been through a tape-out. That’s a small pool in the UK, and it’s the same one Arm, the quantum companies and the defence primes are all fishing in.

The other thing worth noting is how chip companies actually hire, which tends to come in waves rather than at a steady pace. Olix’s first chip is due with customers in the second half of 2027, so the next 12 months are the crunch, and verification demand in particular peaks hard ahead of a tape-out before dropping away. That’s a big reason a lot of experienced chip people seem to have gone independent, and why I think contract talent will quietly do much of the heavy lifting behind these headline raises.

For those hiring, raising the money is no longer the hard part. The hard part is getting the people you need in before your tape-out date, not after it.

For those in the space, particularly anyone with verification, photonics or compiler experience, I don’t think your skills have been this commercially valuable in the UK for a very long time.

As always, I’m very happy to speak with people looking for their next role or those looking to bring people in, so feel free to reach out if you're in either camp.
